title: Mindset
author: Carol S. Dweck
blurb: Psychologist Carol Dweck argues that people hold one of two broad beliefs about their abilities. In a fixed mindset, talent and intelligence are set traits, so every challenge becomes a test of worth and failure feels like a verdict. In a growth mindset, abilities can be developed through effort, good strategies and help from others, so challenges become chances to learn. Drawing on decades of research and examples from school, sports, business and relationships, Dweck shows how these mindsets shape whether people seek challenges, persist through setbacks, accept feedback and celebrate others' success. She explains how praise, parenting, teaching and leadership can push people toward one mindset or the other. Most importantly, she argues that mindsets themselves can change, and offers practical ways to notice your fixed-mindset voice and choose growth instead.

lessons.b: Whether you believe ability is fixed or can grow changes how you interpret almost every challenge you face.

lessons.t: Failure as Verdict or as Information
lessons.b: A fixed mindset treats setbacks and effort as proof of inadequacy, while a growth mindset treats them as the path to improvement.
Even celebrated stars in sports and other fields became great through practice and learning, not talent alone.

lessons.t: Praise the Process, Not the Person
lessons.b: Praising intelligence makes people avoid challenges, while praising effort and strategy makes them seek challenges and persist.

lessons.t: Leaders Who Learn Versus Leaders Who Prove
lessons.b: Fixed-mindset leaders need to look superior and silence bad news, while growth-mindset leaders build teams that learn and adapt.
